titre: The Monte Carlo Roulette Wheel Was Too Regular to Be Honest
accroche: In 1892, Karl Pearson goes through sixteen thousand roulette spins published by a Paris newspaper, and finds chance abnormally well behaved.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1892, the Paris weekly *Le Monaco* publishes, table by table, the numbers that came up at the roulette tables of the Monte Carlo casinos. Karl Pearson, professor of applied mathematics at University College London, obtains four weeks of these records and asks himself a simple question: do these numbers really obey the laws of chance, as the casino claims?

## A Chance Too Regular to Be Honest

Pearson goes through 16,563 spins, which he divides into 148 groups, one per number per week, to measure, group by group, how far the results depart from what a truly random draw would produce. The standard deviation he observes, 7.2, is markedly smaller than the 10.34 expected in theory: the numbers come up too regularly, with too few runs and too few long absences, to be the product of real chance. He calculates that the odds of such a narrowing are about two million to one, and that a month this atypical should, on average, recur only once every one hundred sixty-seven thousand years of continuous play. To check that he has not simply been unlucky enough to land on an out-of-the-ordinary sample, he compares his calculation with a second record, unrelated to his own, kept over four other weeks by an independent correspondent, a Mr. de Whalley: nothing comparable appears in it. Pearson concludes, in the *Fortnightly Review* of 1894, that roulette as played at Monte Carlo is not a scientific game of chance, and urges the French Academy of Sciences to check his calculations, then the French government to close the gaming rooms if it confirms them.

## Neither the Wheel nor Chance, but the Newspaper Itself

Pearson considers a faulty wheel, but he himself notes the mechanical precision of the instrument. More than a century later, the mathematician Adam Kucharski reopens the case and shifts the suspicion: it was not the wheel, but *Le Monaco*. The editors in charge of recording each number at the table, rather than observing them one by one, are said to have preferred to invent most of them. Kucharski explains it this way: someone who makes up a sequence of numbers at random almost always produces a version that is too regular, because he instinctively avoids the long repeated runs that a real draw tolerates without difficulty. This is precisely the anomaly Pearson had measured without knowing its cause: a chance too well behaved to be true.

## One Tool for Two Very Different Culprits

Six years after this episode, Pearson formalizes the chi-square criterion, which generalizes the question he had already asked about roulette: is an observed deviation too large, or here too small, to come from chance alone? The same test that could have unmasked a rigged wheel ended up unmasking journalists too lazy to observe what they claimed to report, which says as much about roulette wheels as about how hard it is, for anyone, to truly imitate chance.

repere.texte: Of the 16,563 spins that he goes through himself (four weeks, 1892), Pearson measures a standard deviation of 7.2 against the 10.34 expected from chance: a regularity so improbable that, by his own calculation, it should recur only once every one hundred sixty-seven thousand years of continuous play.
repere.source: Pearson, The Scientific Aspect of Monte Carlo Roulette, 1894/1897

carte.punch: Pearson judged the Monte Carlo roulette rigged. The real culprit was not the wheel.
carte.idee: In 1892, Karl Pearson goes through 16,563 roulette results published by a Paris newspaper and concludes that Monte Carlo is not an honest game of chance. More than a century later, another explanation emerges: the journalists in charge of recording the numbers are said to have simply made them up.

quiz.question: Why does the anomaly Pearson measures on the Monte Carlo roulette in 1892 not prove, in hindsight, that the wheel was biased?
choix: Because the standard deviation he calculates turns out, on review, to be within the normal limits of chance
Because the casino is said to have set the wheel differently from table to table, which Pearson would not have detected
Because Le Monaco published the results of only one table out of several, which would bias his average
Because the editors in charge of recording the numbers are said, according to later research, to have made them up rather than observed them
quiz.explication: Pearson himself checks the mechanical precision of the wheel: the flaw is not there. Adam Kucharski's later research (2016) shows that the anomaly probably came from the editors of Le Monaco, who are said to have fabricated runs of numbers too regular to be a real random draw, rather than from the wheel itself.
